chunks: Ali ibn Ja'far narrated from his brother Musa (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about the fasting person who tastes drink and food and finds its taste in his throat. He said, 'Let him not do it.' I said, 'If he does it, what is upon him?' He said, 'There is nothing upon him, and he does not have to return (to the beginning of the fast).'

key_terms.فَمَا عَلَيْهِ: what is upon him (what is the ruling)
key_terms.لَا شَيْءَ عَلَيْهِ: there is nothing upon him (no penalty)
key_terms.وَلَا يَعُودُ: and he does not return (does not repeat/make up)

ai.seo_question: Does tasting food or drink break the fast in Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: In this narration from Imam Musa al-Kadhim (AS), the scholar clarifies the distinction between merely tasting and actually breaking the fast, ruling that incidental tasting does not invalidate the fast nor require Qada (making up). This ruling is significant in Shia fiqh for distinguishing between minor acts that do not nullify the fast and those that do, reflecting the principle of ease in worship. The hadith underscores the importance of intention and the physical presence of the substance in the throat for the fast to be considered broken.
